--- course-unit: ch07-reaction-networks status: complete --- # Reaction networks and moment closure {#sec-reaction-networks} ::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"} **Workshop programme**: taught live on Day 2, Session 3. See the [full schedule](../workshop.qmd). ::: Every model so far has been written as *states changing*: a right-hand side for $dS/dt$, a drift and diffusion for $(S,I,R)$, a pair of jump affects. Each time we changed the mathematical setting we rewrote the model. This chapter changes what we write down. Instead of the dynamics of the states, we specify the **flows** — the transmission event and the recovery event, each with the rate at which it fires and the change it makes. That specification is a **reaction network**, and it is enough to generate the ODE, the SDE and the jump process mechanically. It also unlocks something the state view cannot easily give us: equations for the *moments* of the stochastic process, so we can approximate the mean and variance of an ensemble without simulating it. ## Learning goals You will: - write the SIR model as a reaction network of flows rather than state equations; - generate ODE, SDE and jump models from that one specification and check they agree with the hand-written versions of @sec-ordinary-differential-equations, @sec-stochastic-differential-equations and @sec-jump-processes; - derive why the moment hierarchy of a bimolecular reaction does not close; and - apply a normal closure and judge it against a jump-process ensemble; and - solve the master equation directly by finite state projection to obtain quantities a closure cannot, such as the probability of extinction. ## Model assumptions and classification The population, parameters and baseline are unchanged from @sec-jump-processes: a closed, homogeneously mixing $(S,I,R)=(990,10,0)$ with $N=1000$, $c=10.0$, $\beta=0.05$, $\gamma=0.25$, and the composite rate constant $\kappa=\beta c/N$. What changes is the *description*, not the model. A reaction network is not a fourth kind of model sitting alongside the ODE, SDE and jump process: it is a specification from which each of those three is derived. Its classification is therefore inherited from whichever lowering we choose — deterministic and continuous for the ODE, stochastic and continuous for the SDE, stochastic and discrete for the jump process. The moment equations introduced later are a fourth, different object: deterministic equations describing a stochastic process. The one modelling assumption the network itself encodes is **mass action**: the transmission flow is proportional to the number of $S$–$I$ pairs and the recovery flow to the number of infectives. ## Equations A reaction network is a set of reactions, each carrying a rate constant, the species it consumes, and the species it produces: $$ S + I \xrightarrow{\ \kappa\ } 2I, \qquad I \xrightarrow{\ \gamma\ } R. $$ {#eq-ch06-network} From this we read off the two objects that generate everything else. The **stoichiometry matrix** $V$ collects the state change of each reaction as a column, and the **propensity** $a_j(X)$ gives the rate at which reaction $j$ fires in state $X=(S,I,R)$: $$ V = \begin{pmatrix} -1 & 0\\ 1 & -1\\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad a(X) = \begin{pmatrix} \kappa S I\\ \gamma I \end{pmatrix}. $$ {#eq-ch06-stoichiometry} These are exactly the $V$ and $a$ of @sec-stochastic-differential-equations, which is the point: the pair $(V, a)$ *is* the model, and the three settings we have used are three ways of turning it into dynamics. | Lowering | Construction | Chapter | |---|---|---| | ODE | $\dot X = V a(X)$ | @sec-ordinary-differential-equations | | SDE | $dX = Va(X)\,dt + V\operatorname{diag}(\sqrt{a(X)})\,dW$ | @sec-stochastic-differential-equations | | Jump | event $j$ fires at rate $a_j(X)$, adding $V_{\cdot j}$ | @sec-jump-processes | : The same $(V,a)$ generates all three models. {#tbl-ch06-lowerings} ### The chemical master equation and its moments The jump process is the exact model, and its probability distribution $P(x,t)=\Pr\{X(t)=x\}$ obeys the **chemical master equation** $$ \frac{\partial P(x,t)}{\partial t} = \sum_{j} \Big[ a_j(x - V_{\cdot j}) P(x - V_{\cdot j}, t) - a_j(x) P(x,t) \Big], $$ {#eq-ch06-cme} one equation for every reachable state. For a closed SIR population of $N=1000$ that is on the order of $10^{5}$ coupled equations — solvable in principle, and the subject of the finite-state projection appendix, but not something we want to carry around. Rather than the whole distribution, we usually want a few summaries: the mean number infectious, and how variable it is between outbreaks. Multiplying @eq-ch06-cme by $x$ and summing gives an exact equation for the mean, $$ \frac{d\,\mathbb{E}[X]}{dt} = V\,\mathbb{E}[a(X)]. $$ {#eq-ch06-mean} Here is the crux. For recovery, $\mathbb{E}[\gamma I] = \gamma\,\mathbb{E}[I]$: the propensity is linear, so its expectation depends only on the mean. But transmission is **bimolecular**, and $$ \mathbb{E}[\kappa S I] = \kappa\big(\mathbb{E}[S]\,\mathbb{E}[I] + \operatorname{Cov}(S,I)\big) \neq \kappa\,\mathbb{E}[S]\,\mathbb{E}[I] $$ {#eq-ch06-unclosed} unless $S$ and $I$ are uncorrelated. So the equation for the first moments requires the second moments. Writing equations for the second moments brings in the third, and so on: the hierarchy never closes. This also explains something seen in @sec-jump-processes — the mean of an ensemble is *not* the ODE solution. The ODE is what you get by dropping $\operatorname{Cov}(S,I)$ from @eq-ch06-unclosed, and during an epidemic that covariance is strongly negative, which is why the ODE peak sits above the ensemble mean. **Moment closure** cuts the hierarchy off. We keep moments up to some order $m$ and express the ones above $m$ in terms of those below, by *assuming* a distributional shape. The **normal closure** used below sets the third central moments to zero, which is what a multivariate normal distribution would give. The assumption is about the shape of the distribution, not about the model, and it is an approximation that can be good, poor, or numerically catastrophic. ## Julia implementation `@reaction_network` takes the reactions of @eq-ch06-network almost verbatim. This is the same network built in @sec-jump-processes, where it was used only to drive a jump process; here it is the single source for every lowering. ::: {#cell-code-ch06-setup .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using Catalyst using OrdinaryDiffEq using StochasticDiffEq using JumpProcesses using MomentClosure using CairoMakie using StableRNGs using Statistics const N = 1000 const β = 0.05 const c = 10.0 const γ = 0.25 const κ = β * c / N const tspan = (0.0, 40.0) const times = collect(0.0:0.5:40.0) sir_network = @reaction_network begin κ, S + I --> 2I γ, I --> R end ``` ::: {#code-ch06-setup .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ::: The network knows its own species, parameters and stoichiometry, so $V$ of @eq-ch06-stoichiometry need not be typed in by hand. ::: {#cell-code-ch06-structure .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} (species = species(sir_network), parameters = parameters(sir_network), V = netstoichmat(sir_network)) ``` ::: {#code-ch06-structure .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (species = SymbolicUtils.BasicSymbolicImpl.var"typeof(BasicSymbolicImpl)"{SymReal}[S(t), I(t), R(t)], parameters = SymbolicUtils.BasicSymbolicImpl.var"typeof(BasicSymbolicImpl)"{SymReal}[κ, γ], V = [-1 0; 1 -1; 0 1]) ``` ::: ::: ### Three models from one specification Each lowering is a problem constructor applied to the same object. Initial conditions are floating point for the continuous lowerings and integer for the jump process, because a CTMC state counts individuals. ::: {#cell-code-ch06-lowerings .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} parameter_map = [:κ => κ, :γ => γ] u₀_continuous = [:S => 990.0, :I => 10.0, :R => 0.0] u₀_discrete = [:S => 990, :I => 10, :R => 0] ode_solution = solve( ODEProblem(sir_network, u₀_continuous, tspan, parameter_map), Tsit5(); saveat = times) sde_solution = solve( SDEProblem(sir_network, u₀_continuous, tspan, parameter_map), LambaEM(); seed = 20250906, saveat = times) jump_solution = solve( JumpProblem(sir_network, u₀_discrete, tspan, parameter_map; aggregator = Direct(), rng = StableRNG(20250906)), SSAStepper(); saveat = times) (ode_peak = round(maximum(ode_solution[2, :]); digits = 2), sde_peak = round(maximum(sde_solution[2, :]); digits = 2), jump_peak = maximum(jump_solution[2, :])) ``` ::: {#code-ch06-lowerings .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (ode_peak = 158.45, sde_peak = 164.86, jump_peak = 165) ``` ::: ::: Nothing about the SIR model was restated to obtain these three. Changing the network — adding an exposed class, a waning-immunity flow, a second host — would propagate to all three automatically, which is the practical argument for writing flows rather than states. ### Moment equations and closure `generate_raw_moment_eqs(network, 2)` derives the exact equations for the raw moments $\mu_{ijk} = \mathbb{E}[S^i I^j R^k]$ up to order 2. There are nine: the three means, and the six second moments. ::: {#cell-code-ch06-moments .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} raw_equations = generate_raw_moment_eqs(sir_network, 2) (equations = length(equations(raw_equations.odes)), order = raw_equations.m_order, unknowns = string.(unknowns(raw_equations.odes))) ``` ::: {#code-ch06-moments .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (equations = 9, order = 2, unknowns = ["μ₁₀₀(t)", "μ₀₁₀(t)", "μ₀₀₁(t)", "μ₂₀₀(t)", "μ₁₁₀(t)", "μ₁₀₁(t)", "μ₀₂₀(t)", "μ₀₁₁(t)", "μ₀₀₂(t)"]) ``` ::: ::: These nine equations are not solvable as they stand: they refer to third-order moments, exactly as @eq-ch06-unclosed predicted. `moment_closure` supplies the missing relation. ::: {#cell-code-ch06-closure .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} closed_equations = moment_closure(raw_equations, "normal") closure_solution = solve( ODEProblem(closed_equations, [990.0, 10.0, 0.0], tspan, parameter_map), Tsit5(); saveat = times) closure_names = string.(unknowns(closed_equations.odes)) mean_index = findfirst(==("μ₀₁₀(t)"), closure_names) second_index = findfirst(==("μ₀₂₀(t)"), closure_names) closure_mean = closure_solution[mean_index, :] closure_sd = sqrt.(max.(closure_solution[second_index, :] .- closure_mean .^ 2, 0.0)) (retcode = closure_solution.retcode, peak_mean = round(maximum(closure_mean); digits = 2)) ``` ::: {#code-ch06-closure .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (retcode = SciMLBase.ReturnCode.Success, peak_mean = 146.11) ``` ::: ::: `MomentClosure` still builds its `ODEProblem` through the older positional signature, which emits a deprecation notice from ModelingToolkit; the cell above suppresses warnings for that reason alone. ### The whole distribution: finite state projection Moment closure buys the mean and variance cheaply by assuming a shape. The *finite state projection* (FSP) instead solves @eq-ch07-cme directly, on a truncated state space, and returns the full joint distribution — no distributional assumption at all. `FiniteStateProjection.jl` takes the same network object. Two choices make this tractable. Writing recovery as `I --> 0` leaves the state two-dimensional in $(S,I)$, since $R$ is recoverable by conservation; and the population is reduced to $N=50$, because the state space grows as $N^2$ and the exactness is paid for in size. ::: {#cell-code-ch07-fsp .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using FiniteStateProjection const N_fsp = 50 const κ_fsp = β * c / N_fsp const S₀_fsp, I₀_fsp = 46, 4 const fsp_times = [0.0, 5.0, 10.0, 40.0] fsp_network = @reaction_network begin κ, S + I --> 2I γ, I --> 0 end initial_distribution = zeros(N_fsp + 1, N_fsp + 1) initial_distribution[S₀_fsp + 1, I₀_fsp + 1] = 1.0 # all probability on one state fsp_solution = solve( ODEProblem(FSPSystem(fsp_network), initial_distribution, (0.0, 40.0), [:κ => κ_fsp, :γ => γ]), # a symbol map, not a tuple Vern7(); abstol = 1e-10, saveat = fsp_times) expected_infectious = [sum(P[s+1, i+1]*i for s in 0:N_fsp, i in 0:N_fsp) for P in fsp_solution.u] extinction_probability = [sum(P[s+1, 1] for s in 0:N_fsp) for P in fsp_solution.u] (states = (N_fsp + 1)^2, retcode = fsp_solution.retcode, probability_mass = round.(sum.(fsp_solution.u); digits = 8), expected_infectious = round.(expected_infectious; digits = 3), extinction_probability = round.(extinction_probability; digits = 4)) ``` ::: {#code-ch07-fsp .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (states = 2601, retcode = SciMLBase.ReturnCode.Success, probability_mass = [1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0], expected_infectious = [4.0, 7.938, 7.77, 0.137], extinction_probability = [0.0, 0.0383, 0.0841, 0.9193]) ``` ::: ::: Probability mass stays at 1 to eight digits, which is the FSP analogue of the conservation check: the truncated generator still describes a probability distribution, so no probability has leaked off the edge of the projected space. The last row is what neither the ODE, the SDE nor the closure can produce. By $t=40$ the probability that the outbreak has already died out is around 0.92 — a statement about the *distribution*, not about a mean. A closure has no mechanism to represent an atom of probability at $I=0$; solving the master equation does it directly. ::: {#cell-code-ch07-fsp-validation .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} function simulate_small(seed) problem = JumpProblem( fsp_network, [:S => S₀_fsp, :I => I₀_fsp], (0.0, 40.0), [:κ => κ_fsp, :γ => γ]; aggregator = Direct(), rng = StableRNG(seed)) return Array(solve(problem, SSAStepper(); saveat = fsp_times)(fsp_times)) end small_ensemble = Array{Float64}(undef, 2, length(fsp_times), 4000) for k in axes(small_ensemble, 3) small_ensemble[:, :, k] = simulate_small(11_000 + k) end [(time = fsp_times[k], fsp_mean = round(expected_infectious[k]; digits = 3), ensemble_mean = round(mean(small_ensemble[2, k, :]); digits = 3), fsp_extinction = round(extinction_probability[k]; digits = 4), ensemble_extinction = round(mean(small_ensemble[2, k, :] .== 0); digits = 4)) for k in eachindex(fsp_times)] ``` ::: {#code-ch07-fsp-validation .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 4-element Vector{@NamedTuple{time::Float64, fsp_mean::Float64, ensemble_mean::Float64, fsp_extinction::Float64, ensemble_extinction::Float64}}: (time = 0.0, fsp_mean = 4.0, ensemble_mean = 4.0, fsp_extinction = 0.0, ensemble_extinction = 0.0) (time = 5.0, fsp_mean = 7.938, ensemble_mean = 7.939, fsp_extinction = 0.0383, ensemble_extinction = 0.0395) (time = 10.0, fsp_mean = 7.77, ensemble_mean = 7.817, fsp_extinction = 0.0841, ensemble_extinction = 0.0788) (time = 40.0, fsp_mean = 0.137, ensemble_mean = 0.144, fsp_extinction = 0.9193, ensemble_extinction = 0.9165) ``` ::: ::: The FSP means and extinction probabilities agree with 4000 stochastic simulations, as they must: the master equation *is* the process the simulations sample from, so this is a check on the truncation and the numerics rather than on the model. ## Validation The claim to test is that the closure reproduces what an ensemble of jump simulations does. We run 200 independent trajectories, each with its own deterministically chosen seed so the figure is reproducible. ::: {#cell-code-ch06-ensemble .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} function simulate_jump(seed) problem = JumpProblem( sir_network, u₀_discrete, tspan, parameter_map; aggregator = Direct(), rng = StableRNG(seed)) return Array(solve(problem, SSAStepper(); saveat = times)(times)) end ensemble = cat((simulate_jump(6000 + k) for k in 1:200)...; dims = 3) ensemble_mean = dropdims(mean(ensemble; dims = 3), dims = 3) ensemble_sd = dropdims(std(ensemble; dims = 3), dims = 3) @assert maximum(abs.(sum(ensemble; dims = 1) .- N)) == 0 (closure_vs_ensemble_peak_gap = round(maximum(closure_mean) - maximum(ensemble_mean[2, :]); digits = 2), ode_vs_ensemble_peak_gap = round(maximum(ode_solution[2, :]) - maximum(ensemble_mean[2, :]); digits = 2)) ``` ::: {#code-ch06-ensemble .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (closure_vs_ensemble_peak_gap = 0.64, ode_vs_ensemble_peak_gap = 12.98) ``` ::: ::: Population is conserved exactly in every trajectory, as the columns of $V$ require. The two gaps are the quantitative form of the argument after @eq-ch06-unclosed: the closure tracks the ensemble mean far more closely than the ODE does, because it retains the covariance the ODE discards. ::: {#cell-fig-ch06-closure .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} figure = Figure(size = (760, 380)) axis = Axis(figure[1, 1], xlabel = "Time", ylabel = "Infectious") band!(axis, times, ensemble_mean[2, :] .- ensemble_sd[2, :], ensemble_mean[2, :] .+ ensemble_sd[2, :]; color = (:grey, 0.35), label = "Ensemble mean ± sd") lines!(axis, times, ensemble_mean[2, :]; color = :grey25, linewidth = 2, label = "Ensemble mean") lines!(axis, times, closure_mean; color = :firebrick, linewidth = 2, label = "Normal closure") lines!(axis, times, closure_mean .+ closure_sd; color = :firebrick, linewidth = 1, linestyle = :dot, label = "Closure mean ± sd") lines!(axis, times, closure_mean .- closure_sd; color = :firebrick, linewidth = 1, linestyle = :dot) lines!(axis, times, ode_solution[2, :]; color = :steelblue, linewidth = 2, linestyle = :dash, label = "ODE") axislegend(axis; position = :rt, framevisible = false) figure ``` ::: {#fig-ch06-closure .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` Mean and standard deviation of the infectious class from 200 jump-process trajectories (bands), the normal moment closure (solid), and the ODE (dashed). The closure recovers both the mean and the spread of the ensemble; the ODE peak sits above the ensemble mean because it discards the negative covariance between S and I. ::: ::: A closure is an assumption, and assumptions fail. Asking for a log-normal closure on this network produces equations the solver cannot start. ::: {#cell-code-ch06-closure-failure .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} lognormal_retcode = try solve(ODEProblem(moment_closure(raw_equations, "log-normal"), [990.0, 10.0, 0.0], tspan, parameter_map), Tsit5(); saveat = times).retcode catch error Symbol(typeof(error)) end ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html}

Always check the return code, and always compare against simulation before trusting a closure. ## Interpretation and limitations Writing flows rather than states buys three things: one specification instead of three, mechanical access to every lowering, and moment equations that are simply unavailable from a hand-written right-hand side. The costs are real. Moment closure is an *uncontrolled* approximation: unlike reducing a timestep, there is no parameter to refine that guarantees convergence, and the only honest check is comparison with simulation — which is what we were trying to avoid. Closures degrade exactly where stochastic effects matter most, when counts are small, near the start of an outbreak or near extinction. The normal closure can also return negative variances or negative means, both meaningless. And a closure describes the *ensemble*, not any single outbreak: it can tell you the spread of epidemic sizes, but never the probability that an outbreak fades out, which needs the distribution itself — which is precisely what the finite state projection above supplies, at the cost of a state space that grows with the square of the population. Mass action is the network's own assumption. Contact structure, households and age mixing are not expressible as a two-reaction network, and @sec-agent-based-models takes up the individual-level alternative. ## Exercises ### Exercise 1 {#ch07-ex1} Extend the network of @eq-ch06-network to an SEIR model by adding an exposed class $E$, with $S + I \to E + I$ at rate $\kappa$ and $E \to I$ at rate $\sigma = 0.5$. Starting from $(S,E,I,R)=(990,0,10,0)$, generate the ODE and jump lowerings from the single network, and plot the ODE against the mean of 100 jump trajectories. State how the latent period changes the epidemic peak relative to the SIR model of this chapter. ### Exercise 2 {#ch07-ex2} For the SIR network, compare second-order normal closure against an ensemble of 200 jump trajectories at two population sizes, $N=1000$ and $N=100$, holding $\beta$, $c$ and $\gamma$ fixed and scaling $\kappa=\beta c/N$ with the initial condition $(0.99N, 0.01N, 0)$. Report the largest absolute difference between closure mean and ensemble mean in each case, and explain the direction of the change using the argument after @eq-ch06-unclosed. ## Companion materials - [Slides](../slides/chapters/07-reaction-networks.html) - [Pluto preview](../notebook-exports/chapters/07-reaction-networks.html) - [Pluto source](../notebooks/chapters/07-reaction-networks.jl)
